title: Array processing patterns: aggregate, search, count and transform
learningObjectives: Use loops to calculate sums and other aggregates from array elements.
Search arrays with linear search and report whether a value was found.
Count elements that satisfy a condition.
Transform array elements while preserving or deliberately changing the original data.
Handle empty arrays and aggregate overflow according to the problem's requirements.

understand.concept: Array processing is commonly expressed as a traversal over a known number of elements. An aggregate such as a sum combines values; a search looks for a target; a count records how many elements satisfy a predicate; and a transform derives new values. Correct algorithms define the empty-array behavior, valid bounds, result range and whether the original array is modified.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding Array processing patterns: aggregate, search, count and transform helps you reason about program behaviour instead of memorizing syntax. It is useful in exams, debugging and building reliable C applications.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a tool with a precise contract: it has valid inputs, defined operations and observable results.
understand.analogyLimit: An analogy is only an aid; the C standard and the relevant function specifications determine actual behaviour.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Aggregate values

A sum or minimum is calculated by visiting each element and updating an accumulator. Initialize the accumulator deliberately. Choose a type that can represent every intermediate result, not merely the final expected value.

## 2. Search

Linear search checks elements in order until the target is found or the array ends. A useful result convention is to return a found/not-found status and, when found, provide the index separately. Do not use a valid index value as an ambiguous not-found marker without documenting the convention.

## 3. Count matching elements

A count loop increments when an element meets a condition. Ensure the counter can represent the maximum possible number of elements.

## 4. Transform data

A transform may update each element in place or write results to a second array. In-place changes save storage but destroy the original values. A separate destination is useful when the original data must be preserved.

## 5. Empty arrays and overflow

For an empty range, a sum can be defined as zero, while a search returns not found. Define these cases explicitly. Check that accumulators cannot overflow, and never access element zero when the count is zero.

examples.title: Linear search
examples.explanation: This API uses count as a not-found sentinel because valid indices are strictly less than count. Callers must follow that documented convention.

practise.guidedTask: Implement a small C program demonstrating CL4.3. Identify the relevant array or string capacity, valid indices, expected results and failure cases before compiling and testing.
practise.independentTask: Create a second example for CL4.3 that handles a boundary case explicitly. Add tests for empty input, the smallest valid case, the largest valid case and one invalid or oversized case. Explain how your code prevents invalid access.

questions.prompt: What does an aggregate operation such as sum do?
options: Combines values from multiple elements into a result
Changes every element into a string
questions.answer: Combines values from multiple elements into a result
questions.explanation: An aggregate reduces a sequence of values to a summary result.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case number of comparisons in linear search over N elements?
questions.explanation: If the target is absent or last, each element may be checked.

questions.prompt: What should be defined for an empty array before computing an aggregate?
options: The intended empty-input result and whether any access is skipped
questions.answer: The intended empty-input result and whether any access is skipped
questions.explanation: Algorithms should explicitly define behavior for an empty range.

options: A transform that updates the original array elements
A transform that always allocates a second array
A transform that sorts the source file
questions.answer: A transform that updates the original array elements
questions.explanation: In-place processing modifies the original storage.

questions.prompt: Why must the accumulator type be chosen carefully?
options: Intermediate sums may exceed the range even when individual elements fit
The compiler chooses it from the array name
All sums are automatically arbitrary precision
questions.answer: Intermediate sums may exceed the range even when individual elements fit
questions.explanation: Every intermediate result must be representable.
